citations.review_text: I just don't understand the love for this game. The story and setting are interesting, but the actual gameplay, just caring packages around while trying to avoid BTs and MULEs is just tedious. If you love simulating an Amazon delivery driver, but without a vehicle, who has to strap boxes on your back, arms, legs and hips, you'll love this game.
If you love the sound of a baby crying and constant beeping while crab-walking around invisible monsters in the rain, this game is also perfect for you.

This would be a great movie. It's a horrible game.

Im about 5 hours in and I just cant stand how utterly boring and confusing this game is, its well marketed and I enjoy open world post apocalyptic game but this is just straight up trash... there are just too many elements to the game that go unexplained and im left guessing as to what to do and how to approach situations like avoiding detection by bts, finding cover from the rain which destroys your packages etc... the story seems interesting but the gameplay made it far too painful for me to endure long enough to see it through. The characters themselves lack depth, seem far fetched and the baseline is just corny and weird. If I wanted to watch a guy shower and take a ♥♥♥♥ id would have gone to public sauna. Stumbling around and falling with a bunch of boxes stuck to my back is just enfuriating, the terrain and graphic are meh, felt absolutely no immersion or connection to the abstract form of gameplay and story telling either. Just straight up boring steaming pile of trash Im perplexed that this game has so many positive reviews and that they are asking for like 120aud for the part 2... ridiculous.

citations.review_text:
THIS IS THE SAME REVIEW FROM THE OG Death Stranding. This game is mostly the same, but better!

Updated thoughts at the bottom!

--------------------------------------------------------------

Lots of people: Walking Simulator.

Me: Delivery Sim, Walking/Hiking and Driving, building roads and items to make things easier. Paranormal and terrorist threats in your way. Oh, and don't forget the rain that ages you and cargos in your journey.
And there is SOME combat, mostly in the story and stolen cargo deliveries. HAAH.

Also, random baby on an expensive beautiful artificial womb machine companion. Adorable.
(If I pass by a baby sign cause of other players and hear Norman say, "Someones happy" with the baby laughing ONE MORE TIME, I swear-)

The game that got me addicted to 'Don't be so Serious", "BB's Theme" and the famous trailer song back in the days, "Path" from Apocalypse.

Optimization, Graphics, Environments/Weather mechanics? (Especially in ultrawide!) Looks so Amazing <3
Ran super smooth on a laptop I had (Razer Blade 14) and current setup? Even better!

Soundtrack: TRON/Stranger Things vibes, and some vocal indie types play here and there. (If you know about those Ethereal "otherworldly calm voice" types lmao (2009 times...)

Singleplayer? Actually... some Undirected CoOP. Structures, sign emotes, dropped cargo and vehicles left behind by you or others can appear in other people's games. It can be quite hilarious or extremely helpful. especially amazing to see how many people have made it in some hard to reach or secret places.
A lot of stuff even have a like system to see how many people have reacted to said items and found your help awesome!
If you are worried that stuff that are not useful to you appear, you can get rid of them! or log off.
There is even a DS Profile system and privacy info choices.

Road and Structures made to keep your items safe, cross hazards and hook line to far reaches, generators to energize your electronic mobility? Can be upgraded …

I've dipped in and out of Death Stranding for months, never devoting more than a couple of hours at a time, but every time I do, I really enjoy what I find here.  The game is completely unique, and quite hard to describe.  A "walking simulator" this is not, it's something much more rich.

The story and world seem strong, and I'm curious about how things pan out.  I'm a little frustrated by the lack of weapons three chapters in, but the stealth forced has been quite good.  Then there's the social system whereby you come across things other players have left that leave this single player game feeling uniquely connected and alive.  

It's hard not to recommend Death Stranding when on sale, because it's such a unique experience.  I haven't fully formed an opinion of the game yet, but I do know it's a good game and that I'm enjoying it, which is what matters.

citations.review_text:
That's a great blend of a walking simulator and an adventure game.
You can step into a post-apocalyptic as a true courier.
It's nice to see well-known actors in the game.
The story is interesting, set in a unique sci-fi world envisioned by Hideo Kojima.
Although the game is quite long and using vehicles becomes more practical than walking in the second half of the game. In my opinion, walking is the essence of this series.
I’m not a fan of that type of multiplayer games where you don’t see other players in real-time, only traces of their activity, like structures or signs - because I’m never quite sure if it’s all real or fake.

A slow start but once things get going it can really pull you in. A delivery man on the surface but underneath there is so much more. The story will raise a lot question that give way to suspicions. As you progress the world itself grows and you are constantly reminded that you're not alone in this journey. The signs and structures from other players is a fragment of their journey they left behind for you to find. The relationships that Sam builds and his growth as a character gives plenty of reason to continue delivering packages. The technological advances make pushing forward all the more worth it. In the end it will all click together, you were given the pieces of the puzzle and the picture is displayed upon completion. The final piece was also the first and with it a final answer to a question you didn't ask. 

BB liked that.

Greatly enjoyed the experience of this one, it does have flaws in terms of story that irk me a little bit, vehicle controls could be better in most cases, but other than that, has been a long time since I played something that feels like a videogame with a compelling story and tasteful Online implementation. Walking simulator with a grand story and rich lore, I would recommend to try it out, it is worth it.

This game is truly one of a kind.

I really like it's peacefulness in nature being alone and what most people hate about this game walking.
Helping other players by building structures but not actually seeing them is a interesting mechanic which i personally like.

This game is not for everyone as some find it boring and call it a walking sim but it is mostly because they played for 5 hours wich the gameplay at that time is walking from A to B but after you reach episode 3 the true beauty of this game starts to shine. 

Over all really loved the game even after finishing the story.

It's been years since I've played a Metal Gear game, but I'm so happy that Kojima still has the ability to surprise me with his vibrant storytelling. A beautiful exploration of the nature of life and death that seamlessly weaves layers of metaphor together into a solid knot. Yes, I stole the central metaphor of the game for this review. Getting to this franchise 6 years late I feel like the world was very lived in, but what a cool concept that I can show up late and get to stand on the shoulders of those who played before me. Extremely innovative and unique gameplay that is so much more than just "being a delivery man". Really great performances from most (not gonna name names) of the central cast (Troy Baker you know I'm not talking to you buddy). Overall, a wholly unique experience with a beautiful story to tell. Everything you'd hope for a Kojima game to be.

citations.review_text: Really want to recommend this game- it's extremely fun and engaging and I'm hooked on the plot. However, every hour or so the game crashes due to an "access violation" and no amount of troubleshooting seems to have fixed it. It's really taking me out of enjoying the game to be in the middle of a run and hear the dreaded Windows error sound.

Exceptional game, but not nearly for everyone.

Death Stranding is one of my favorite games that I've recently played, but it took me a while to get into it. I tried playing the game on the PS5, first, through PS+. It was a fine experience, but I dropped it about halfway through. Its just hard to boot up the game again after some time away. 

Later on, I bought it on PC. Again, I dropped it halfway through. This time was because of a lack of haptic feedback. Seriously, play the game with a plugged-in controller. It greatly changes the experience. 

The story is incredible. Plot twists I never saw coming, and actual stakes. For me, the game ran really well.  On some games, my computer struggles to hit 100+ fps. (Namely subnautica 2, overwatch, rivals, etc...) but with this, I consistently got 144 fps with high settings. 

The game's pacing is all over the place, so you need to be patient with the game. Don't expect an action game. Expect a walking simulator. One that makes you REALLY want to walk.

9/10

Death Stranding has been one of the weirdest, most confusing and unique games I've ever played, and I would be lying if I said I wasn't absolutely captivated by it. The whole premise, the amount of surreal and striking imagery, the landscapes, the weird characters, the insanely long intro and ending sequences, all of it left an extremely lasting impression on me, which is much more than I can say for most games of this caliber.

The story is kind of what I imagine would be the result if you mixed a Simmons novel and a Lynch movie. Not all of it holds up, some of the writing is inconsistent, some of it is deliberately ambiguous, some of it doesn't make sense, but to me, all of this is easily forgiven due to how mindbending and delightfully human the end result is. If it didn't have those things, I feel like the end result would have ultimately been much more formulaic.

What I can't forgive so easily are issues with the gameplay. Previously, I've often seen people make fun of DS for being a 40h walking simulator, and I kind of just parroted their talking points. Having played it myself now, the game really does manage to take something as simple as walking through landscapes and makes that fun and interesting. To me, the game was at its best when it was just me, my cargo, and a scenic, barren landscape to walk or drive through. In those moments, the game was honestly the perfect thing to play after a long day at university. What created a lot of frustration and (probably intended) friction for me were the combat and stealth sections. It's possible that I didn't engage with the mechanics to their fullest and made things harder for me than I needed to as a result, but to me, those aspects were always just something I had to push through to get back to the stuff I liked. claims.claim: The game features an asynchronous multiplayer system where players can use structures, roads, and supplies left behind by other players to navigate the world.

citations.review_text: When I discovered this game back in 2019 or 2020, people on the internet said it was boring, "basically a walking simulator," and even friends and family who play video games felt the same way. But on May 3, 2026, I gave it a try, and in just two hours of gameplay, it became my favorite game. The gameplay definitely isn't for everyone, which is understandable since it might be boring for some people who prefer games with a bit more action. It's worth clarifying that there is action in the game, but it also depends on how the person plays it, as everyone has their own way of playing video games. The game combines exploration, stealth, tactical combat, and resource management. Later in the game, you can see the story explained, which is incredible, along with the evolution of the protagonist, Sam Porter Bridges, played by Norman Reedus. This brings me to the topic of acting. The entire cast was truly amazing. In every scene and with every character's behavior, you can really see what each one is like. It's true that the other characters have somewhat silly names, but they are also explained within the game with meaning. The in-game music, mostly by Low Roar, is also incredible; it truly gives the game the vibe it deserves. The music kicks in at specific points in the game, where it does its job perfectly, setting the mood. The game features an asynchronous online system, which I find one of the most fun aspects. Multiple players can place structures that can help you from time to time, and the signals add to the fun. If I enjoyed this game so much, I'm sure I'll love Death Stranding 2: On The Beach.

It starts slow, and that's a filter, not a flaw. It worked exactly as designed: the people still calling it a walking simulator quit before the game had finished clearing its throat. You carry things across a broken country. The weight is real, the balance is real, the ground argues with you the whole way. Then a stranger you will never meet leaves a ladder at the exact spot where you gave up, and the whole thesis arrives without a line of dialogue. "Delivery boy" is what you call that if you left before it meant anything. Nothing here gets solved alone. The roads are paved with materials other players donated and cannot use themselves, and every route you take was made passable by somebody who got nothing back for it. And when a fight turns bad and you're out of everything, a supply box lands beside you, sent by someone you crossed paths with and forgot. No message attached. Somebody just remembered you were out there. Connection isn't the theme of this game, it's the physics. Half the complaints are just a description of the first two hours, written by people who never saw the other forty. The twists hit hard. The allegories run deeper than the marketing ever suggested. The final sequence isn't a cutscene, it's a film, and it earns every minute of its length. If a game has to justify itself immediately, the problem isn't the game. The last game that got this far into me was Planescape: Torment, a quarter of a century ago. Same charges then: too slow, too strange, too much talking. Everyone who stayed came out different. Death Stranding 2 might be the first game I buy at full price in twenty years. That's the review.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the opening hours as slow-paced, featuring lengthy cutscenes and a dense amount of unfamiliar terminology and world-building concepts before the core gameplay fully opens up.

citations.review_text:
Death Stranding — ★★★★½ (8.4/10)

Directed and designed by Hideo Kojima, this action-adventure game refuses to try pleasing every player, blending delivery mechanics, exploration, indirect cooperative building, and heavily maximalist storytelling into an experience genuinely about human connection in a collapsed world. Set in a devastated future America after the "Death Stranding" event tore apart the boundary between the living and the dead, players take on Sam Porter Bridges, a courier working to link isolated settlements into a national communication network, attempting to rebuild social and political bonds. The core idea is genuinely striking — rather than making the hero someone who kills everything in his path, the game makes him someone who carries boxes and crosses terrain to reconnect people, a smart redefinition of heroism where service, care, connection, and cooperation become central actions rather than narrative afterthoughts. That said, the world is dense with interlocking terminology — BTs, Timefall, Chiralium, BB, DOOMS, ♥♥♥♥ Demens — which gives the game real identity but creates a real barrier to entry that can be hard to clear early on. The story unfolds across long chapters that start noticeably slow before gradually expanding into a family and metaphysical conspiracy about extinction, birth, death, and connection, using long cinematic sequences, in-game emails, interviews, and readable files that make the game feel closer to a sprawling interactive novel — its best quality is tying that grand idea directly to the moment-to-moment gameplay, since every successful delivery isn't just a task but an act that reconnects part of the world to the network, though the storytelling occasionally over-explains, with some scenes delivering too much information or re-clarifying ideas the game already gestured toward. The core gameplay loop — moving across difficult terrain with a limited, shifting cargo load — is one of the game's most original ideas; balanci…

I'm not a die-hard H. Kojima fan. I've only played the original Metal Gear Solid and, much later - MGS V: The Phantom Pain. And now, after another long break, I finally picked up Death Stranding: Director's Cut.

You don't have to be a Kojima fan to appreciate the man's talent, but you'd have to be an absolute idiot not to recognize his genius. His games are known for two things: incredibly well-crafted stories and cinematics that can easily last for hours. Death Stranding is no exception—if anything, it perfectly reinforces that reputation. It's also one of the most unique games I've ever played. Many people jokingly call it a "DPD Simulator", but let's be honest—where else are you going to find a game that lets you throw Norman Reedus' bodily fluids at your enemies??

The game was a slow starter for me. Right from the start, it felt incredibly "console-like." You select something, press a button, another confirmation window pops up, you press another button, another menu appears, then a short cutscene plays before you're finally allowed to move again. There were menus everywhere, tons of small text, and absolutely no handholding when it came to the story. BTs? Beaches? BBs? DOOMS? The game simply throws all these terms at you and expects you to figure things out yourself.

Your first deliveries are made entirely on foot. A brand-new world, constant rain, rough terrain, strange structures, and long, winding routes between destinations. It definitely took me a while to get used to everything. But then... the game suddenly clicked.

By the time I was wrapping up the Eastern Region, I finally felt comfortable. I had a motorcycle, a decent amount of equipment, some grenades... yet one question kept running through my head: "When do I finally get some proper guns?" Well... not anytime soon. And even when firearms eventually become available, the game constantly encourages you to think twice before pulling the trigger.

There's actually a very logical reason for that.

K…

If you told me a game about being an apocalyptic Amazon delivery guy with a baby in a jar would be a masterpiece, I’d have laughed in your face. But man, Death Stranding Director's Cut somehow hooks you right in. It brings back that hardcore survival vibe where every single step actually matters. The Director's Cut adds awesome toys like jetpacks and cargo catapults, making building roads and moving giant stacks of boxes insanely satisfying. It’s this weird but perfect mix of totally relaxing zen and pure panic when those creepy invisible ghosts show up.

That being said, you definitely need some serious patience for it. The first few hours are basically just a confusing, super long movie, and you will rage when you trip over a dumb rock and dump all your hard work down a hill. Dealing with the rain literally destroying your stuff can also feel like a massive chore sometimes. But if you can stick it out past the crazy slow start, it turns into one of the most addicting, unique games out there.

I'm not a die-hard H. Kojima fan. I've only played the original Metal Gear Solid and, much later - MGS V: The Phantom Pain. And now, after another long break, I finally picked up Death Stranding: Director's Cut.

You don't have to be a Kojima fan to appreciate the man's talent, but you'd have to be an absolute idiot not to recognize his genius. His games are known for two things: incredibly well-crafted stories and cinematics that can easily last for hours. Death Stranding is no exception—if anything, it perfectly reinforces that reputation. It's also one of the most unique games I've ever played. Many people jokingly call it a "DPD Simulator", but let's be honest—where else are you going to find a game that lets you throw Norman Reedus' bodily fluids at your enemies??

The game was a slow starter for me. Right from the start, it felt incredibly "console-like." You select something, press a button, another confirmation window pops up, you press another button, another menu appears, then a short cutscene plays before you're finally allowed to move again. There were menus everywhere, tons of small text, and absolutely no handholding when it came to the story. BTs? Beaches? BBs? DOOMS? The game simply throws all these terms at you and expects you to figure things out yourself.

Your first deliveries are made entirely on foot. A brand-new world, constant rain, rough terrain, strange structures, and long, winding routes between destinations. It definitely took me a while to get used to everything. But then... the game suddenly clicked.

By the time I was wrapping up the Eastern Region, I finally felt comfortable. I had a motorcycle, a decent amount of equipment, some grenades... yet one question kept running through my head: "When do I finally get some proper guns?" Well... not anytime soon. And even when firearms eventually become available, the game constantly encourages you to think twice before pulling the trigger.

There's actually a very logical reason for that.
